kurals.tamil:
எள்ளாமை வேண்டுவான் என்பான் எனைத்தொன்றும்
கள்ளாமை காக்கதன் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaamai venduvaan enbaan enaiththondrum,
Kallaamai kaakkathan nenju.
kurals.meaning: Anyone who wishes never to be held in contempt must guard his own heart so that it never even plots to take, by stealth or trickery, anything at all that belongs to another, however small.
kurals.elementary: Nobody wants to be laughed at or called a cheat. The way to make sure that never happens is to keep a guard at the door of your own mind, so that even the idea of sneaking away something that isn’t yours — even a pencil — never gets in.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by locating fraud (kaḷavu) not in the hand but in the heart (neñcu): the verb is kākka, “let him guard,” and its object is the mind itself. Valluvar’s motive clause is social and reputational — eḷḷāmai, “not being scorned” — which fits the householder-and-ascetic audience of the Tuṟavaṟaviyal section, where public trust is the currency of a moral life. The word eṉaittoṉṟum (“anything whatsoever”) forecloses the familiar rationalisation that small frauds do not count, anticipating the Aristotelian claim that theft admits no virtuous mean. Commentators from Parimēlaḻakar to Mu. Varadarasan read kaḷḷāmai as covering not only burglary but every covert appropriation, including short-changing and deceit in dealings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do not covet the wealth of any man!”
hinduism.explanation: The very first verse of the Isha Upanishad tells the seeker to see everything as belonging to the Lord and, on that basis, never to hanker after anyone else’s property.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts place the prohibition at the level of desire and extend it to any wealth at all, not just large thefts.
hinduism.source: Isha Upanishad 1 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE vol. 1)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on inner restraint regarding others’ property; the Upanishad’s ground is theological (all is the Lord’s) rather than reputational.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that honesty is tested in trivial matters; a person who cheats in small things reveals a character that will cheat in large ones.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s “anything whatsoever” (eṉaittoṉṟum): no fraud is too small to matter.
christianity._accuracy_note: Excellent match on the ‘even the smallest thing’ point; lacks the Kural’s emphasis on guarding the heart and on public contempt.

islam.quote_or_event: “So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”
islam.explanation: Surat az-Zalzalah teaches that on the Day of Judgement even the tiniest deed, good or bad, will be brought to light.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that any wrong is too small to count, and ties wrongdoing to eventual exposure.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘no wrong is too small’ logic; not specifically about fraud, and the exposure is eschatological rather than social contempt.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let the property of your fellow be as precious unto you as your own”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yose’s maxim in the Mishnah asks a person to value a neighbour’s possessions exactly as he values his own, which rules out any scheme to take them.
judaism.tie_back: Both locate honesty in an inner disposition toward others’ property, cultivated before any act.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit: an internal attitude that makes fraud unthinkable; lacks the reputational motive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who in this world takes nothing that is not given to him, be it long or short, small or big, good or bad — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the truly noble person as one who never takes what is not freely given, regardless of its size or value.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada’s “small or big” is the same sweep as the Kural’s eṉaittoṉṟum — honesty admits no exceptions.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the scope of non-stealing; the Kural adds the motive of avoiding contempt.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how the old herdsman Battus saw Mercury driving off Apollo’s stolen cattle and was bribed with a cow to keep silent. Mercury returned in disguise, offered a cow and a bull for information, and Battus betrayed the secret at once; Mercury turned him into a stone, a lasting emblem of the informer.
greek_mythology.explanation: A small, greedy gain made through complicity in theft and double-dealing leaves Battus a permanent object of scorn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s warning that even a petty fraudulent gain leads to lasting disgrace.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate: the theme of small corrupt gain bringing lasting disgrace fits, but the myth is about bribery and betrayal more than guarding one’s own heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder; for all of these and suchlike things imply by their names that they are themselves bad”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, having defined virtue as a mean, stops to insist that some acts, theft among them, have no right amount; any instance of them is simply wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: Supplies the philosophical logic behind “anything whatsoever”: there is no acceptable quantity of fraud.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel on ‘no amount is acceptable’; Aristotle does not focus on guarding the mind or on reputation.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே பிறன்பொருளைக்
கள்ளத்தால் கள்வேம் எனல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullaththaal ullalum theethe piranporulaik,
Kallaththaal kalvem enal.
kurals.meaning: Even to think in one’s mind, “I will take his property from him by cunning,” is itself a wrong.
kurals.elementary: Imagine thinking, “When no one is looking, I’ll trick my friend out of his toy.” Even if you never do it, just planning it is already a bad step, because every wrong action begins as a thought.
kurals.university: Valluvar moves culpability upstream from act to intention: uḷḷattāl uḷḷalum tītē — “even the thinking with the mind is evil.” The phrase kaḷḷattāl kaḷvēm (“we shall steal by craft”) specifies the content of the forbidden thought as a deliberate scheme, not a passing temptation, which is important for the ethical claim. This parallels the Tenth Commandment’s ban on coveting, the Buddhist teaching that mind precedes action, and the Gita’s account of how dwelling on objects breeds desire. Commentators note the psychological realism: fraud requires premeditation, so the only reliable defence is to refuse the premeditation itself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain from mere contemplation of desirable things to attachment and then to consuming desire.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say the danger starts in thought; dwelling on another’s wealth is the first link in the chain toward fraud.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on thought as the seed of wrongdoing; the Gita speaks of sense objects generally, not fraud specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit…”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what defiles a person comes from inside the heart, listing thefts, covetousness and deceit among evils that start as inner thoughts.
christianity.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: theft and deceit are born in the heart before the hand.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match; explicitly names theft and deceit as originating in inner thought.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allāh will bring you to account for it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that God judges what lies hidden within a person as well as what is displayed.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s claim that a concealed intention to defraud is already morally weighed.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on accountability for inner states; not specific to fraud, and Islamic tradition (per 2:286) qualifies liability for mere passing thoughts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house; thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his man-servant, nor his maid-servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.”
judaism.explanation: The last of the Ten Commandments forbids not an act but a desire directed at a neighbour’s property.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the inner wish to take another’s goods itself a transgression.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; note that some rabbinic authorities hold the prohibition is violated only when desire leads to action.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada’s opening verse makes mind the source of every action and its consequences.
buddhism.tie_back: Grounds the Kural’s claim that the fraudulent plan in the mind is already the root of the harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on mind-first ethics; general rather than fraud-specific.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Glaucon’s tale in Plato’s Republic, the shepherd Gyges finds a ring that makes him invisible; secure from detection, he uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and seize the kingdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend asks what a person would do if he could take anything without being seen, exposing whether honesty is inner or merely fear of exposure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural answers Gyges: the scheme formed in the unseen mind is already the wrong, detection or not.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Republic II, 359c-360b (legend of the Ring of Gyges)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematically apt (hidden intention versus visible act); the story itself is a thought experiment, not a moral about thought-crime.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.”
philosophy.explanation: Kant opens the Groundwork by locating moral worth entirely in the will, not in outcomes.
philosophy.tie_back: Converse of the Kural: if goodness lies in the will, a will set on fraud is already bad before it acts.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (tr. T. K. Abbott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Philosophical parallel on intention as the seat of morality; Kant is not discussing theft here.

kurals.tamil:
களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம் அளவிறந்து
ஆவது போலக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kalavinaal aakiya aakkam alavirandhu,
Aavadhu polak kedum.
kurals.meaning: Wealth gained through fraud may seem to swell beyond all measure, but it will perish — and take more with it than it brought.
kurals.elementary: It’s like a soap bubble: a stolen treasure puffs up bigger and bigger and looks amazing, and then — pop! — it’s gone, and it can even splash away the things you already had.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the paradox of āvatu pōla, “as if growing”: fraudulent gain has the appearance of prosperity but not its substance. The phrase aḷaviṟantu is read two ways by commentators — as “beyond measure” describing the apparent growth, or (with Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar) as the ruin exceeding its natural limit and consuming even legitimately held wealth. Either way, Valluvar denies the fraudster even a prudential victory. The same instability of ill-gotten wealth is a commonplace across Hesiod, Proverbs, Jeremiah and the Qur’an, suggesting a widely shared moral-economic intuition that dishonest gain lacks durable foundations.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Held in bondage by hundreds of desires, and driven by lust and anger, they strive to accumulate wealth by unjust means, all for the gratification of their senses.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the demoniac character as heaping up wealth by unlawful means; the surrounding verses trace this path to ruin and lower births.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts expose unjust accumulation as a false prosperity that ends in downfall.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear match on wealth by unjust means; the ruin is stated in the surrounding verses (16.16, 16.19-20) rather than this verse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah compares wrongly gained wealth to eggs a bird broods over but never hatches: the promise of increase never comes to fruition.
christianity.tie_back: Identical logic to “as if growing, it perishes”: the apparent increase of unjust riches is illusory.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on apparent growth ending in loss.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh destroys interest and gives increase for charities.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an contrasts usury, which seems to multiply wealth, with charity, which seems to reduce it; God reverses both appearances.
islam.tie_back: Same paradox as the Kural: exploitative gain that looks like growth is actually headed for destruction.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the ‘apparent growth, real loss’ structure; concerns riba (usury) rather than fraud in general.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished; But he that gathereth little by little shall increase.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts wealth gained through emptiness or dishonesty, which dwindles, with patiently earned wealth, which grows.
judaism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s claim that fraud-wealth decays while honest wealth endures.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; ‘vanity’ (hevel) is broader than fraud but is commonly read as dishonest gain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as rust arising from iron eats away the base from which it arises, even so, their own deeds lead transgressors to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares wrongdoing to rust that grows out of iron and then consumes the very metal that produced it.
buddhism.tie_back: Mirrors the reading of aḷaviṟantu in which fraud-wealth destroys even the wealth one already had.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking image of self-consuming wrong; general wrongdoing rather than fraudulent wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue, as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that wealth taken by force or by deceitful speech is quickly withdrawn by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost a paraphrase of the Kural: fraudulent wealth stays only a little while and brings the house down with it.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 320-326 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, explicitly including theft ‘through his tongue’ (fraud).

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy argues that riches are never truly a person’s own: they belong to Fortune, who hands them out and takes them back as she pleases, so no one should rest security or identity on them.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius stresses how unstable external wealth is and how foolish it is to trust it.
philosophy.tie_back: Strengthens the Kural’s point: if even honest wealth is unstable, wealth gained by fraud rests on nothing at all.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: shares the instability-of-wealth theme but does not single out fraudulent gain.

kurals.tamil:
களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல் விளைவின்கண்
வீயா விழுமம் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kalavinkan kandriya kaadhal vilaivinkan,
Veeyaa vizhumam tharum.
kurals.meaning: An ingrained craving for gain by fraud, when it finally bears its fruit, yields sorrow that never ends.
kurals.elementary: Wanting to cheat is like planting a thorn bush because its flowers look pretty. When it grows up, the thorns keep poking you, and you can never get rid of them.
kurals.university: Kaṉṟiya kātal — a desire that has become hardened or habitual — is the subject, and the agricultural verb viḷaivu (ripening, harvest) sets up the karmic metaphor: fraud is a seed whose fruit is vīyā viḻumam, “unperishing affliction.” The emphasis on habit links this couplet to 286 and 288, where Valluvar treats fraud as a character formed by repetition. The imagery of delayed but certain ripening is close to the Dhammapada’s description of evil deeds that seem sweet until they ripen. Commentators split between reading the sorrow as this-worldly (disgrace, punishment) and as extending into later births; the adjective vīyā allows both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names greed among the three doors to hell and says these passions degrade the self.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘hardened craving’ for fraudulent gain is exactly lobha (greed), and its fruit is lasting ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on greed leading to lasting ruin; not specific to fraud.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes deceitful gain as sweet at first and painful in its aftertaste.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s movement from desire to a bitter harvest (viḷaivu).
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on the sweet-then-bitter consequence of deceit; ‘undying’ is not stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever betrays, [taking unlawfully], will come with what he took on the Day of Resurrection. Then will every soul be [fully] compensated for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that whoever misappropriates goods will carry them to Judgement, where every soul receives its due.
islam.tie_back: The fraudulent gain becomes a lasting burden, like the Kural’s ‘unperishing affliction’.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear link between unlawful taking and lasting consequence; context is the misappropriation of war booty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For all that do such things, even all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the LORD thy God.”
judaism.explanation: After commanding honest weights and measures, the Torah declares that anyone who deals dishonestly is an abomination to God.
judaism.tie_back: The lasting harm of the Kural is framed here as enduring estrangement from God.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the gravity of commercial fraud; the ‘undying sorrow’ element is implied rather than stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So long as an evil deed has not ripened, the fool thinks it as sweet as honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the consequences of an evil deed stay hidden until they ripen, and then they bring grief.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s harvest metaphor: wrong ‘ripens’ (viḷaivu) into sorrow.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in structure and imagery of ripening; general evil rather than fraud.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Pindar’s version, Tantalus, a guest at the gods’ table, stole nectar and ambrosia and gave them to his mortal drinking companions; for this he was punished forever, with a huge stone hanging over his head.
greek_mythology.explanation: A theft driven by craving and pride is repaid with punishment that never ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic image of the Kural’s vīyā viḻumam — sorrow that does not die — as the harvest of theft.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Theft leading to eternal punishment fits well; the myth carries additional themes (hubris, abuse of divine hospitality).

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates argues that doing injustice is worse than suffering it, and that the wrongdoer who escapes punishment is the most wretched of all, because his soul stays diseased.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the real harm of wrongdoing is inside the wrongdoer: a lasting corruption of the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Gives a philosophical account of why the Kural’s sorrow is ‘undying’: the damage is to the self, not just to fortune.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good conceptual parallel on lasting inner harm; Plato addresses injustice generally.

kurals.tamil:
அருள்கருதி அன்புடைய ராதல் பொருள்கருதிப்
பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்கண் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulkarudhi anbudaiya raadhal porulkarudhip,
Pochchaappup paarppaarkan il.
kurals.meaning: Those who covet another’s goods and wait for his moment of carelessness cannot be people of love who cherish compassion.
kurals.elementary: A real friend helps you when you drop your lunch money. Someone who waits for you to drop it so they can grab it can’t be kind at the same time — the waiting-to-grab heart pushes the kindness out.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts two inner orientations: aruḷ karuti, “holding grace (compassion) in regard,” and poruḷ karuti, “holding another’s wealth in regard.” The fraudster’s signature act is poccāppu pārttal — watching for the other person’s forgetfulness or unguardedness — which Valluvar treats as incompatible with aṉpu (love). The couplet ties this chapter to the preceding ones on Aruḷuṭaimai (compassion), showing that for Valluvar honesty in dealings is not a separate commercial rule but a consequence of compassion. Kant’s shopkeeper, the hadith of the wet grain, and Micah’s schemers lying awake all describe the same failure: treating another person’s vulnerability as an opportunity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…compassion for all living entities; freedom from covetousness; gentleness; modesty…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists compassion and freedom from covetousness side by side among the divine qualities.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita pairs exactly what the Kural pairs: compassion (aruḷ) and the absence of coveting others’ wealth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close conceptual pairing; the Gita lists them as co-present virtues rather than arguing their incompatibility with fraud.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, after citing ‘Thou shalt not steal’ among the commandments, sums them all up as love, which cannot harm a neighbour.
christianity.tie_back: Same logic as the Kural: love and scheming against a neighbour’s goods cannot coexist.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on love excluding harm; lacks the specific image of watching for another’s lapse.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Prophet put his hand into a heap of grain and found the lower part wet, he said: “Why did you not place this (the drenched part of the heap) over other eatables so that the people could see it? He who deceives is not of me (is not my follower).”
islam.explanation: The seller hid damaged grain where buyers would not notice, relying on their lack of vigilance; the Prophet declared such deception outside his community.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s target: profiting from the other party’s unguarded moment (poccāppu).
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: fraud that exploits the buyer’s inattention; the hadith frames it as exclusion from the community rather than as lack of compassion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Woe to them that devise iniquity And work evil upon their beds! When the morning is light, they execute it, Because it is in the power of their hand. And they covet fields, and seize them…”
judaism.explanation: Micah condemns those who lie awake plotting to seize others’ property and act as soon as the chance comes.
judaism.tie_back: Captures the Kural’s schemer who covets and waits for the right moment to take.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on premeditated coveting and opportunism; the victims here are defrauded by power rather than by inattention.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, accepts only what is given, lives not by stealth but by means of a self that has become pure.”
buddhism.explanation: Describing the virtue of a monk, the Buddha contrasts a life of stealth with one lived by a purified self.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s stealthy watcher and the Buddha’s ‘life by stealth’ are the same figure; purity of heart excludes both.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good on stealth versus inner purity; does not explicitly mention compassion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, when gods and mortals were settling their portions, Prometheus divided an ox deceptively: the meat and fat innards hidden in the ox’s stomach, and the bare bones wrapped in glistening fat. He invited Zeus to choose, hoping he would be fooled by appearances; Zeus in anger withheld fire from mankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: A trick in the dividing of shares, relying on the other party taking the surface at face value, poisons the relationship between gods and humans.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s point that a dealer who counts on the other side’s oversight destroys goodwill.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate: a clear fraud in apportioning, but Prometheus acts out of sympathy for humans, which complicates the ‘no compassion’ point; Hesiod says Zeus saw through the trick.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is always a matter of duty that a dealer should not over charge an inexperienced purchaser”
philosophy.explanation: Kant’s example of the honest shopkeeper: exploiting a buyer who cannot judge the price is the plain wrong that honesty forbids.
philosophy.tie_back: The inexperienced purchaser is the person whose unguarded moment the Kural’s fraudster is waiting for.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (tr. T. K. Abbott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Precise match on not exploiting another’s vulnerability in trade; Kant grounds it in duty rather than love or compassion.

kurals.tamil:
அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார் களவின்கண்
கன்றிய காத லவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Alavinkan nindrozhugal aatraar kalavinkan,
Kandriya kaadha lavar.
kurals.meaning: Those in whom the love of gain by fraud has hardened cannot keep their conduct within the bounds of measure.
kurals.elementary: A scale in a shop is supposed to measure fairly. Someone who loves cheating is like a scale with a broken spring — it can’t stay steady, and it keeps tipping the wrong way.
kurals.university: Aḷavu (“measure, limit”) is the key term of the second half of the chapter (286-289), and Valluvar plays on its near-rhyme with kaḷavu (“fraud, theft”). Commentators differ on what aḷavu means: Parimēlaḻakar takes it as the ascetic’s limited livelihood, Mu. Varadarasan as thrift or contentment, others as the rule of right conduct. The rhyme itself makes the point that fraud is a failure of measure, which is why honest weights and measures are the concrete test in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, the Qur’an and the Buddhist suttas. The couplet repeats kaṉṟiya kātal from 284, presenting fraud as a habit that eats away the ability to keep within limits.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is regulated in his habits of eating, sleeping, recreation and work can mitigate all material pains by practicing the yoga system.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches moderation (yukta) — a measured life — as the foundation of spiritual discipline.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s ‘regulated’ person is the one who keeps within aḷavu; the Kural says the fraud-lover cannot.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the ideal of measured conduct; does not mention fraud or theft.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a set determination to become rich traps people in desires that drag them beyond all restraint.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes an entrenched desire for gain that destroys a person’s ability to live within bounds.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on entrenched greed overwhelming restraint; not specifically about fraud.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to those who give less [than due], Who, when they take a measure from people, take in full. But if they give by measure or by weight to them, they cause loss.”
islam.explanation: Surat al-Mutaffifin condemns traders who demand full measure for themselves but short-change others.
islam.tie_back: The literal failure of measure (aḷavu) through fraud in weights, the concrete form of the Kural’s abstract point.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong on fraud as a violation of measure; the Kural’s ‘measure’ is also moral and not only commercial.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not have in thy bag diverse weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thy house diverse measures, a great and a small. A perfect and just weight shalt thou have; a perfect and just measure shalt thou have…”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids even keeping two sets of weights, one for buying and one for selling.
judaism.tie_back: The fraudster’s ‘great and small’ weights are exactly a refusal to stand by a single, fixed measure.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct match on fraud as the corruption of measure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He abstains from running messages… from buying and selling… from dealing with false scales, false metals, and false measures… from bribery, deception, and fraud.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the virtues of the monk, the Buddha lists refusal to use false scales and measures and refusal of deception and fraud.
buddhism.tie_back: Makes honest measure part of the definition of virtue, as the Kural does.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct match on false measures and fraud; the list is framed as monastic virtue.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cut down Ceres’ sacred oak for his own use. Ceres sent Famine to him, and he became insatiably hungry: he consumed all his wealth, repeatedly sold his daughter Mestra, and in the end devoured his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Someone who seized what was not his is punished with an appetite that has no limit.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of the Kural’s point that the fraud-lover cannot remain within any measure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate: boundless appetite after an act of sacrilegious taking; the myth concerns impiety more than fraud.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…virtue must have the quality of aiming at the intermediate.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines moral virtue as hitting the mean between excess and deficiency.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s mean is a close counterpart to Valluvar’s aḷavu; the fraud-lover has lost the ability to aim at it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on measure as the core of virtue; Aristotle does not link it to theft here.

kurals.tamil:
களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை அளவென்னும்
ஆற்றல் புரிந்தார்கண் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kalavennum kaarari vaanmai alavennum,
Aatral purindhaarkan il.
kurals.meaning: The dark cleverness called fraud is not found in those who have chosen the strength called measure.
kurals.elementary: Some people are clever in a sneaky, shadowy way. But a person who has learned to be happy with a fair share has a brighter kind of strength, and the sneaky cleverness simply has no room to live in them.
kurals.university: Kār aṟivu — literally “black knowledge” — is Valluvar’s striking name for fraud: an intelligence that is real but darkened, directed at deception rather than understanding. He opposes to it aḷavu eṉṉum āṟṟal, “the power called measure,” so that restraint is framed not as weakness but as a form of strength. The contrast anticipates Aristotle’s distinction between practical wisdom and mere cleverness (deinotēs), which can serve bad ends. Textual note: some online editions print the last word-group as புரிந்தார்கண்ட இல்; the reading புரிந்தார்கண் இல் given here follows Tamil Surangam and thirukkural-thamizh.org and fits the metre.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among all modes of purification, purity in (the acquisition of) wealth is declared to be the best; for he is pure who gains wealth with clean hands, not he who purifies himself with earth and water.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu ranks honesty in acquiring wealth above every kind of ritual purity.
hinduism.tie_back: The person of ‘measure’ in the Kural is the one with clean hands in money matters; dark cleverness has no place there.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on honest acquisition as a supreme virtue; lacks the ‘dark knowledge’ contrast.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says true profit is godliness joined to contentment, not accumulation.
christianity.tie_back: Contentment is the ‘strength of measure’; it removes the motive for the dark cleverness of fraud.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on contentment as the antidote; lacks the Kural’s specific image of dark intelligence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even [i.e., honest] balance. That is the best [way] and best in result.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands honest measure and calls it both morally best and best in its outcome.
islam.tie_back: Affirms, like the Kural, that honest measure is a strength rather than a loss.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on measure as the superior path; the Qur’an’s measure is commercial, the Kural’s also moral.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment with one’s portion.
judaism.tie_back: The contented person has the ‘strength of measure’ and so no use for fraud’s dark cleverness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on contentment as true strength; fraud is not explicitly mentioned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks contentment above every material possession.
buddhism.tie_back: Contentment is the Kural’s aḷavu; where it is present, the urge to defraud does not arise.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on contentment as wealth; fraud is implied, not stated.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the newborn god uses his cunning to steal Apollo’s cattle and lie about it. When Zeus orders a reconciliation, Hermes gives Apollo the lyre, receives honours over herds in exchange, and swears he will never steal from Apollo again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The trickster’s dark cleverness is turned into lawful exchange once he accepts a fixed and agreed share.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s point from the other side: fraudulent cunning ends once someone accepts measure (an agreed, fair portion).
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate and complicated: Hermes’ trickery is celebrated rather than condemned, and he is never truly punished.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus tells his students to behave in life as at a banquet: when a dish is passed to you, reach out and take a moderate share; if it passes you by, do not grab after it; if it has not yet reached you, do not send your desire ahead of it.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic ideal is a disciplined measure in taking, grounded in accepting one’s portion.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s aḷavu is the banquet-guest’s moderation, which leaves no room for grabbing by stealth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on measure in taking; does not address fraud directly.

kurals.tamil:
அளவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சத் தறம்போல நிற்கும்
களவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சில் கரவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Alavarindhaar nenjath tharampola nirkum,
Kalavarindhaar nenjil karavu.
kurals.meaning: Just as virtue lives steadily in the hearts of those who know measure, deceit lives steadily in the hearts of those who have learned fraud.
kurals.elementary: Your heart is like a room. If you practise being fair, fairness moves in and makes itself at home. If you practise cheating, sneakiness moves in instead — and whoever lives there decides how you act.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on precise parallelism — aḷavu aṟintār / kaḷavu aṟintār (“those who know measure / those who know fraud”) — with the verb niṟkum (“stands, abides”) serving both halves. The point is that virtue and deceit (karavu, “concealment”) are both settled dispositions formed by what one has come to “know” through practice. This is close to Aristotle’s claim that we become just or unjust through our dealings with others, and to the Gospel image of the heart as a treasury from which good or evil is brought out. It also explains 284 and 286: once fraud is ‘known’ in this habitual sense, concealment becomes the heart’s standing condition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among them, the open rogues (are those) who subsist by (cheating in the sale of) various marketable commodities, but the concealed rogues are burglars, robbers in forests, and so forth.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu classifies thieves the king must restrain and puts dishonest traders among them, treating fraud in the market as a settled way of life.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s ‘rogues who subsist by cheating’ are the Kural’s kaḷavu aṟintār, people for whom deceit has become a livelihood and a habit.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on commercial fraud as a settled way of life; lacks the virtue/deceit parallel of the heart.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes the heart as a storehouse whose contents determine a person’s words and deeds.
christianity.tie_back: Same two-sided structure as the Kural: virtue dwells in one kind of heart, deceit in the other.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close structurally; not specific to fraud.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and when a thief steals, then he is not a believer at the time of stealing…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that faith and theft cannot occupy the heart at the same moment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the heart as holding either faith/virtue or deceit, but not both together.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the mutual exclusion of virtue and theft in the heart; does not stress habituation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “This is as Shmuel said: It is prohibited to deceive people, and even to deceive a gentile.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud’s principle of geneivat da’at (‘theft of the mind’) treats creating false impressions as a form of theft, and lists many everyday examples.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis, like Valluvar, see deceit (karavu) as fraud’s inner form, forbidden even when no goods change hands.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 94a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on deceit as a kind of theft; lacks the Kural’s habituation parallel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says character fills up gradually, one small deed at a time.
buddhism.tie_back: Explains how kaḷavu aṟintār come to have deceit settled in the heart: little by little, through repeated practice.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good on gradual habituation; its twin verse 122 gives the virtuous side.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’ maternal grandfather Autolycus is said to have surpassed all men in thievery and in the oath, a skill given to him by Hermes, whom he honoured with sacrifices.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer presents skill in theft and tricky oaths as a settled excellence of character, almost a gift of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An example of the Kural’s kaḷavu aṟintār: for Autolycus deceit has become a stable second nature.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates deceit as settled character; Homer is admiring rather than condemning, which is the opposite of Valluvar’s tone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “by doing the acts that we do in our transactions with other men we become just or unjust”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle teaches that moral character is formed by habit, and that justice or injustice is built up through how we deal with others.
philosophy.tie_back: The same two-sided account of habituation as the Kural: repeated honest dealing makes virtue settle in, and repeated fraud makes deceit settle in.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, including the context of transactions.

kurals.tamil:
அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர் களவல்ல
மற்றைய தேற்றா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Alavalla seydhaange veevar kalavalla,
Matraiya thetraa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who know no way of living other than fraud will be destroyed in the very act of their measureless deeds.
kurals.elementary: If the only trick you know is cheating, it’s like a player who only knows how to foul — sooner or later, right in the middle of the game, they get caught and sent off.
kurals.university: The couplet says the fraudster’s ruin is not deferred but comes āṅkē — “right there,” in the act itself. The phrase kaḷavu alla maṟṟaiya tēṟṟātavar (“those who do not understand anything other than fraud”) describes a person whose repertoire has narrowed to one method, which completes the habituation argument of 288. Plato gives a striking parallel: a completely unjust person could not act at all, because cooperation depends on some remnant of justice. Acts 5’s account of Ananias, struck down while misrepresenting a sale, is the most literal illustration of perishing ‘right there.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who enjoys such gifts without offering them to the demigods in return is certainly a thief.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls anyone who only takes and never gives back a thief, cut off from the cycle of reciprocity that sustains life.
hinduism.tie_back: The person who knows nothing but taking has broken the order that sustains him, which parallels the Kural’s self-destroying fraudster.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: defines a thief by non-reciprocity, but does not state immediate ruin; chosen as the best available Hindu parallel.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ananias and Sapphira sold a property, secretly kept back part of the price, and presented the rest as the whole. When Peter confronted him, “Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost”.
christianity.explanation: A deception about the price of a sale is followed at once by death.
christianity.tie_back: The most literal parallel to āṅkē vīvar — the fraudster perishes ‘right there,’ in the act.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on immediate ruin from fraud; the narrative frames the lie as against the Holy Spirit.

islam.quote_or_event: “And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice and do not deprive the people of their due and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption.”
islam.explanation: The prophet Shu’ayb warns the people of Madyan, notorious for short-weighting, to stop; the Qur’an goes on to tell how they persisted and were destroyed (11:94).
islam.tie_back: A community that knew nothing but fraud in measure perished in its measureless deeds, as the Kural warns.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong: persistent fraud in weights leading to destruction; collective rather than individual.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The getting of treasures by a lying tongue Is a vapour driven to and fro; they [that seek them] seek death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says treasure gained by lies is a passing vapour, and those who pursue it are in effect pursuing their own death.
judaism.tie_back: Matches the Kural: those committed to deceitful gain are destroyed by the very pursuit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on self-destruction through deceitful gain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who destroys life, utters lies, takes what is not given, goes to another man’s wife, and is addicted to intoxicating drinks — such a man digs up his own root even in this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that one who takes what is not given destroys his own foundations in this very life.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Digs up his own root even in this world’ matches the Kural’s ruin āṅkē — here and now.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on this-worldly self-destruction through theft.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sisyphus, remembered as the craftiest of men for his many deceptions (including cheating death), is seen by Odysseus in the underworld endlessly pushing a huge stone uphill, only for it to roll back each time.
greek_mythology.explanation: A life built entirely on trickery ends in labour that achieves nothing and never ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘those who know nothing but fraud’ find their cleverness turned into futile, self-defeating action.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate: an image of crafty deceit ending in futility; the punishment is eternal rather than immediate, and his deceits are not mainly commercial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for had they been whole villains, and utterly unjust, they would have been utterly incapable of action.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that even a band of thieves needs some justice among its members to act; total injustice would make action impossible.
philosophy.tie_back: A philosophical form of the Kural’s claim: someone who knows only fraud undermines the very conditions for successful action and fails in the act.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual parallel on pure injustice being self-defeating.

kurals.tamil:
கள்வார்க்குத் தள்ளும் உயிர்நிலை கள்ளார்க்குத்
தள்ளாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kalvaarkkuth thallum uyirnilai kallaarkkuth,
Thallaadhu puththel ulagu.
kurals.meaning: For those who defraud, even life in the body will fail them; for those who never defraud, even the world of the gods will not fail.
kurals.elementary: Cheaters can lose even the simple things everyone needs, like a safe life. People who stay honest are promised the biggest prize of all, like a door to heaven that will always open for them.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with an antithesis built on one verb, taḷḷu (“to fail, to reject”): life itself (uyirnilai, the soul’s stay in the body) ‘fails’ the kaḷvār, while the world of the gods (puttēḷ ulaku) ‘does not fail’ the kaḷḷār. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first clause vividly as ‘even their own life shuns the thief.’ Textual note: some online editions repeat கள்வார்க்குத் in the second line, but the antithesis requires கள்ளார்க்குத் (“to those who do not defraud”), which is the reading of Tamil Surangam, thirukkural-thamizh.org and the standard commentaries. The contrast of this-worldly collapse with heavenly reward parallels 1 Corinthians 6:10, the Chandogya Upanishad’s list of those who ‘fall,’ and the Talmud’s first question at the heavenly court.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who steals gold, or drinks liquor, or goes to bed with his teacher’s wife, or kills a brāhmin—these four are lost. Also lost is the fifth—one who keeps company with such people.”
hinduism.explanation: In its teaching on the paths of souls after death, the Chandogya lists the thief of gold among the gravest sinners, who are ‘lost’ (patanti, ‘fall’).
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties theft to the soul’s downfall, in contrast to the higher worlds reached by the virtuous (5.10.7).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on theft leading to the soul’s fall; the reward half appears in the surrounding verse 5.10.7.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists thieves, the covetous and extortioners among those shut out of God’s kingdom.
christianity.tie_back: The negative mirror of the Kural’s second line: heaven fails the defrauder and, by implication, stays open to the honest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on exclusion from heaven for theft and extortion; Paul’s next verse (6:11) adds the possibility of cleansing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do they not think that they will be resurrected For a tremendous Day - The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?”
islam.explanation: Straight after condemning those who give short measure, the Qur’an reminds them of the Day of Judgement.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets fraud in dealings against one’s final destiny.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on linking commercial fraud to ultimate fate; the reward of the honest comes later in the surah (83:22-28).

judaism.quote_or_event: “…when a person is brought to judgment for the life he lived in this world, they say to him in the order of that verse: Did you conduct business faithfully?”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that the first question asked at the heavenly court is whether one dealt honestly in business.
judaism.tie_back: Makes honesty in dealings the first key to the world beyond, as the Kural makes non-fraud the guarantee of the gods’ world.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: honest dealing as the first criterion of heavenly judgement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Some are born in the womb; the wicked are born in hell; the devout go to heaven; the stainless pass into Nibbana.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada sets out the different destinies that follow different kinds of conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s two-way contrast of downfall for wrongdoers and heaven for the upright.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good structural match on differing destinies; not specific to fraud.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod contrasts the prosperity and peace the gods grant the just with the ruin they send on the crooked.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets divine favour for the straight dealer against collapse for the crooked one.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-227 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on justice rewarded by the gods; the reward is earthly prosperity rather than a heavenly world.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates declares that the gods do not neglect the good, in this life or the next.
philosophy.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s confidence that the honest will not be failed, even beyond death.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on security for the good after death; concerns goodness in general rather than honesty in dealings.
